title: Ibn Battuta’s travels, 1325–54
summary: A judge from Tangier sets out for Mecca and keeps going for twenty-nine years: Cairo, Persia, East Africa, Delhi, the Maldives, China, then home by way of Granada and the Sahara to Mali.

sources.title: H. A. R. Gibb (trans.), Ibn Battuta: Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354 (1929), Internet Archive
The Travels of Ibn Battuta, Berkeley ORIAS

events.label: First hajj at Mecca
events.text: He left Tangier at twenty-one, alone, meaning to make the pilgrimage and come home. He reached Mecca in 1326 and the road went on for nearly thirty years.

events.label: Kilwa, the southernmost point of the journey
events.text: The Rihla calls Kilwa one of the most beautiful and well-built towns in the world, a city of stone and coral on an island, and its sultan renowned for giving. It was the southern end of the Swahili gold trade, and the furthest he went.

events.label: Delhi: eight years as a qadi for Muhammad bin Tughluq
events.text: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq made him a judge, a qadi, with a large salary and a house. He fell into debt, then under suspicion, and lived through some bad years before the sultan sent him off as ambassador to China.

events.label: The Maldives: qadi of the islands
events.text: Shipwreck and robbery on the way to China left him in the Maldives, where he stayed nine months as chief judge, married into island families, and tried to make the women cover their breasts. A quarrel with the vizier sent him on his way.

events.label: Zaytun (Quanzhou), the Chinese port
events.text: He calls it Zaytun and says its harbour was one of the greatest in the world, with a hundred large junks and small ones past counting. The Rihla is one of the few eyewitness accounts of a Chinese port in the Yuan years.

events.label: Damascus in the year of the Black Death
events.text: The plague reached Damascus in 1348. The Rihla describes Muslims, Jews and Christians processing together to pray, fasting for three days, and puts the dead at some 2,400 a day. He had come from Gaza, where it was already killing.

events.label: The court of Mansa Sulayman, Mali
events.text: The sultan of Mali sent him three loaves of bread, a piece of beef fried in baobab oil and a gourd of curds, which Ibn Battuta thought a poor welcome and said so. He praised the people all the same for their justice, the safety of their roads, and their hatred of injustice.

events.label: Ibn Battuta died in Morocco, c. 1369
events.note: The place is unrecorded; Tangier and Fez are the usual guesses.
events.text: He dictated the Rihla at Fez in 1355–56 and died in Morocco about 1368–69. Nobody recorded where, so the skull stands in the country, not on a town.

alternatives.label: Died at Tangier, his birthplace, where a tomb is shown
alternatives.text: He was born at Tangier and a tomb is shown there, though the place of his death is unrecorded.
